summary: NTU Singapore authors propose PaperCompiler, a paper-to-code pipeline. It first grounds implementation evidence from an ML paper with provenance labels (paper-supported, inferred, delegated, unresolved). It then 'compiles' that evidence into repository-level specifications: reconciled requirements with non-degradation constraints, file ownership, cross-file dependencies and per-file contracts. Finally it generates files under those contracts. On 90 Paper2CodeBench papers with o3-mini generation and o3-mini-high judging, it scores higher than PaperCoder, ChatDev and MetaGPT on three LLM-judged 1-5 fidelity protocols.

claims.claim: PaperCompiler improves reference-based fidelity by 13.8% (3.647 -> 4.152) over PaperCoder, plus smaller reference-free (4.562 -> 4.777) and P2C-Ex (4.535 -> 4.728) gains.
claims.evidence: Table 1, 90 papers in three 30-paper conference subsets; per-paper win ratios in Fig. 4. Every score is an o3-mini-high LLM judgment on a 1-5 scale; no generated repository is executed or tested against reported results (Appendix A). The judge is not validated against human ratings in this paper.

claims.claim: High-severity evaluator critiques fall from 13.2% to 6.1%.
claims.evidence: Table 3: 337/2561 vs 162/2649 items. The severities are assigned by the LLM evaluator; humans assigned the failure categories. API/schema mismatches rise from 2.3% to 4.0%.

claims.claim: PaperCompiler beats end-to-end systems AutoP2C and AutoReproduce.
claims.evidence: Table 2 on a 10-paper random subset: ref-based 4.263 vs PaperCoder 3.825, AutoReproduce 2.650, AutoP2C 2.088. Small sample; uses 1.71M tokens vs PaperCoder's 0.98M.

claims.claim: Each component (reconciliation, context slicing, contracting) contributes.
claims.evidence: Table 4 (9 papers, one generation each): only reference-based scores favour the full system (4.38 vs 3.86-4.11). On ref-free and P2C-Ex, ablations match or beat it (w/o Context Slicing 4.72/4.74 vs 4.57/4.42). The authors then choose to focus on the metric that supports them.

patterns.note: Persistent, structured specifications that bind each requirement to an implementing file beat free-form plans as the hand-off between stages (LLM-judged).
Explicit requirement reconciliation with provenance and non-degradation constraints; removing it costs most on reference-based fidelity (Table 4).
Ownership graph and cross-file dependency contracts, within a single repository; API/schema mismatches actually rose.
Entire evaluation rests on an LLM judge (o3-mini-high) with no human validation reported.

methodology.sample: 90 papers (ICLR/ICML/NeurIPS 2024, 30 each) from Paper2CodeBench; 10-paper subset for end-to-end comparisons; 9-paper ablation.
methodology.baselines: PaperCoder (re-run under matched settings), ChatDev and MetaGPT (likely carried over from the PaperCoder paper and not re-run), AutoP2C, AutoReproduce.
methodology.models: o3-mini generation, o3-mini-high evaluation; a single, now-dated backbone.
methodology.variance: Std. across papers reported; multiple sampled judge outputs averaged (8 in ablation). One generation per paper, with no variance across generation seeds (acknowledged).
methodology.ablations: w/o reconciliation, context slicing, contracting (9 papers).
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; author repositories from 2024 are likely in training data.

standards.artifacts: No code link in text or metadata; prompt excerpts and example outputs in Appendices E-F.

biases.detail: All fidelity scores and severities come from o3-mini-high, with no human agreement check or execution-based validation.
'Faithful' implementation is claimed, but nothing is executed and reported results are not reproduced (Appendix A).
10-paper end-to-end comparison and 9-paper ablation, each generated once.
The ablation discussion discounts the two metrics where ablations win and focuses on reference-based scores.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: OpenAI o3-mini as backbone and judge; no author vendor ties.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding section found.
coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating their own method with an LLM judge; intellectual self-evaluation, no commercial COI.

verdict_reason: The idea of persistent, file-level specs with provenance is relevant to SDD, and the abstract numbers match Tables 1 and 3. But all evidence is an unvalidated o3-mini-high judge, nothing is executed, generation is single-backbone and single-run, the domain is Python ML papers only, the ablation is mixed, and there is no code.
applicability: A concrete design hint for spec-driven development, not proven practice. The idea that transfers is to compile a feature spec into per-module contracts: requirement -> owning module/class, interfaces it must expose, cross-module dependencies, and 'must not simplify' constraints, each tagged with provenance (spec-stated vs inferred vs unresolved). Then hand each generation step only its slice. For the Java backend team this maps onto a spec -> per-repo/per-service contract (OpenAPI/JSON Schema, ownership in CODEOWNERS-like metadata) across the several repositories. The explicit 'unresolved' bucket is a good trigger for human consultation on domain-specific content rules. Caveats: one repo, Python, LLM-judged only, and API/schema mismatches actually increased. A Java team should pair any such contracts with compile and contract tests rather than rely on judge scores. Host-agnostic, since the contracts are plain files.
